title: Reading 1 · Tracing the evidence
description: Воздухообмен в школе, архив паромной конторы и эксперимент с числовыми подсказками.
instructions: Allow 60 minutes for all three passages. Answer questions 1–40. Select one option or copy words from the passage, following the limit in each instruction. For TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN compare the statement with the information. For YES/NO/NOT GIVEN compare it with the writer’s views.

sections.title: A route for classroom air
sections.body:
A. In a classroom on a still afternoon, an open window can seem a disappointing instrument. Air scarcely moves across the nearest desk, let alone as far as the blackboard. The caretaker at Larch Street School used to take this as a sign that natural ventilation had failed. Yet a group of building researchers proposed a different diagnosis. The trouble was not that the air lacked somewhere to enter. It lacked a useful route out. Warm air that rose to the ceiling collected above the tops of the windows, leaving the children seated in a much slower exchange of air below.

B. To investigate, the team fitted two neighbouring classrooms with an experimental channel. Each room already had a narrow opening near the floor on its shaded side. The new channel rose outside the opposite wall, rather like a tall hollow book standing on its end. The inner face of the channel carried a dark absorber. Sunshine warmed this surface, which in turn heated the air immediately beside it. As that air rose, it drew room air through a high grille. Cooler outside air could then enter through the low opening. No part of this account requires the moving air to touch the children directly. The pressure difference between the two ends of the route does most of the work.

C. There was a practical objection. A small bird entering the channel from above could become trapped where it narrowed. The builders fitted a mesh cap over the upper outlet. They also needed a way to close the route on cold days. A sliding shutter was placed at the room end of the high grille, within reach of a teacher using a short handle. A visitor might have guessed that the cap and shutter had the same purpose. In fact, the first remained in place throughout the year, whereas the second belonged to the school's daily routine. On the drawing the arrows show the movement of air, not the movement of either fitting.

D. The experiment was designed to distinguish fresh air from a mere sensation of coolness. On six empty afternoons the researchers released an equal quantity of a harmless tracer into each room. A small mixing fan ran briefly and was switched off before any measurements began. They recorded the time required for the tracer concentration to fall to half its starting value. A shorter interval indicated faster replacement with outside air. Thermometers at the desks supplied a separate record. One room had its channel open while the other had it closed. The next day the settings were exchanged. This crossover reduced the chance that a permanent difference between the rooms would be mistaken for an effect of the channel.

E. During strong sunshine, the open channel roughly halved the clearance time relative to the closed one. During overcast weather the difference was slight. Strikingly, desk temperatures on the sunny days changed very little. A body can feel cooler in moving air, but that observation did not entitle the researchers to describe the channel as a refrigerator. Its measured success lay in replacing air. Nor could the experiment establish how well a crowded classroom would perform. Empty rooms allowed the tracer test to proceed without disturbance, but removed the heat generated by a class and the interruptions caused by a door opening between lessons.

F. After the trial the caretaker found a thin strip of felt loose along the edge of one shutter. On windy evenings it made a noise that children in a neighbouring club had described as a whistle. Reattaching the felt stopped the sound. The fault would have been invisible in the concentration record, since the tracer tests took place before the club arrived. The team's report therefore recommended recording complaints alongside the instrument readings. It did not treat every complaint as proof of a defective design. Instead it advised tracing each one to a particular component or operating condition before altering a building.

G. The governors asked whether the same channel should be installed in all the school's rooms. The engineers declined to produce a single answer. Some rooms faced a yard overshadowed by a taller building, and others already had two usable openings on opposite walls. Each group needed its own assessment. The first useful purchase, the team suggested, was not a set of channels but a few days of observation in the rooms themselves. A teacher who knew which doors were normally shut could sometimes explain more about the path of the air than a drawing prepared before the school opened.

sections.title: What the ferry books counted
sections.body:
A. In the attic of a former ferry office at Bellwater lay twenty narrow books bound with string. Each page carried the name of a landing place, a date and a list of payments in an untidy, economical hand. The first researcher to describe the books called them a passenger register. That description travelled much further than the books themselves. It appeared in a museum label and then in a local history, where the daily totals supported a story of steadily increasing travel. When historian Lina Vale tried to reproduce the graph in the local history, however, she found that the pages answered a rather different question.

B. Vale had worked in accounts before returning to university. She noticed that a clerk had drawn a red line under the last payment on each page and carried the sum into a box headed 'cash in hand'. There was no equivalent box for the total number carried. Coins mattered to the clerk because they had to be handed over at the end of a shift. A passenger with a pass contributed nothing to the cash box and was ordinarily absent from the list. Conversely, one line might represent payment for several people. Reading every line as one traveller therefore introduced two distinct errors, which need not cancel each other out.

C. A second source made the omissions visible. The town's school kept a book of attendance certificates issued to pupils living across the river. On some mornings as many as twenty certificates had been stamped on the far bank, whereas the ferry book recorded only nine separate payments. The children travelled on a term pass paid for in advance by the town. Vale could now identify one group of missing passengers. She still could not turn the difference between certificates and payments into a count of everyone on board. A pupil might stay home through illness and an adult pass holder had no reason to ask for a school certificate.

D. Paper conservator Arun Mehta approached the problem through the pages themselves. Some pages that seemed to belong to consecutive days were slightly narrower than their neighbours. Mehta matched a pattern of tiny holes in one page to a pattern on a loose sheet filed with repair invoices. Together they formed one edge of a sheet that had been folded before it was cut. The sheet listed three days of payments from the previous month. Its position in the bundle had been decided by someone sorting papers years later. For six weeks of the record, page order alone could no longer be trusted as a guide to the sequence of trips.

E. A third collaborator, economist Rosa Chen, was interested in a charge introduced for carrying bulky parcels. Following the new charge, average revenue per payment rose. A tempting inference was that passengers had become wealthier. Chen instead compared entries on market mornings with entries on other mornings. The increase was concentrated on market mornings, when baskets and sacks were commonly taken to stalls across the river. The extra money was consistent with more payments for parcels. The comparison did not establish whether the owners themselves had more income. It did, however, identify a policy change that could alter the shape of a graph apparently concerned with people.

F. To present the revised interpretation the museum considered replacing its first graph with an estimate of total crossings. The researchers resisted. Where independent evidence was available they could give a minimum: there had to be at least as many pupils present as there were individually stamped certificates for that day. For several winter weeks even that evidence was absent, because damp had destroyed a portion of the school book. Drawing a smooth line between the surviving points would hide a change in the quality of evidence. The museum eventually used separate panels for payments and pupils and left unrecorded days blank.

G. The books did not lose their historical value when their original label came off. They became unusually informative about the practical demands of the ferry business. A clerk who distinguished parcels from people was not failing to anticipate the questions a future historian might ask. He was recording the distinctions needed to collect money and explain a shortage at the end of a shift. Historians often begin with the categories they want to count. Bellwater suggests the reverse procedure: first try to understand which decisions the writer of a record expected it to support. Only then decide what, beyond those decisions, it might reasonably show.

sections.title: When a number changes the evidence
sections.body:
A. Suppose a visitor to a market is asked to guess the weight of a stone. Just before answering, she hears someone say that another stone weighs twelve kilograms. Her guess may be higher than it would have been if she had heard the number two instead. A familiar explanation is that the first number provides a starting point from which the visitor adjusts too little. But the same observation is compatible with another story. The visitor may believe that the two stones come from the same collection and that the other weight is therefore worth taking seriously. An experiment that merely finds different guesses following different numbers has not yet distinguished these accounts.

B. A team at North Hill College built a task in which a number could be useful on some rounds and useless on others. Participants estimated the number of beans in a closed jar after seeing a photograph of it. On the screen beside the photograph a dial stopped at a number. A blue border meant the dial had been set using a sample of jars from the same workshop. A grey border meant that its value came from a random draw. Participants learned these rules in a short demonstration. No participant was allowed to handle the jar. That restriction kept the available evidence similar across sessions, although it also made the task less like estimating quantities in a kitchen.

C. The researchers varied the border and the number independently. Within each border condition, half the photographs appeared with a comparatively high number and half with a low one. No participant saw the same photograph twice. Across the group, however, every photograph occurred under every combination of conditions. That arrangement matters. A high estimate might reasonably be made for a jar photographed from below, which can make it appear large. If that photograph always came with a high dial reading, an apparent influence of the reading could really be an influence of the camera. Distributing photographs across conditions prevents that particular confusion at the level of the group.

D. The high dial readings generally produced higher estimates with both borders, but the gap was wider with blue borders. One interpretation is that participants partly used what they had been told about the dial. Yet the continued gap with grey borders left room for a second influence. In a follow-up task, new participants had to name one visible feature of the jar before making an estimate. Those who saw high readings tended to mention its broad shoulders. Those who saw low readings more often mentioned the narrow neck. Naming a feature did not prove that attention to the feature caused the final estimate. It did suggest a route by which an irrelevant number could change the evidence that a person actively considered.

E. There was an alternative interpretation of the follow-up. Perhaps people had already chosen their estimates and afterwards selected a feature that would justify them. Asking for a feature first established the order of the recorded responses. It did not establish the order of the underlying thoughts. To examine this possibility the team proposed briefly covering the dial before showing the photograph and recording eye movements from the first moment the image became visible. The proposal was left for a later study. It would be a mistake to cite those eye movements as confirmation of either interpretation, because none had actually been measured.

F. The findings attracted interest from a museum that asks visitors to estimate the age of everyday objects. Its designers considered removing all numbers from the gallery. The researchers thought this an unnecessarily broad response. Removing the maker's date from an object would deprive visitors of relevant evidence. Removing an unrelated date printed on the wall beside it might be sensible. What the designers needed first was an inventory that distinguished useful cues from accidental neighbours. Even then they would have to test the revised display. A visitor who had spent the morning looking at ancient pottery might bring a starting point into a room that contained no printed dates whatsoever.

G. There is a wider lesson here for the design of advice. People are often urged to ignore an initial estimate as though it were a switch they could turn off. The North Hill task suggests a more practical question: what independent evidence would lead to a different estimate? A visitor who noticed only the shoulders of a jar might compare its neck and base before giving an answer. Such a procedure is worth testing. The evidence described here does not show that it works, and it certainly does not show that every initial estimate should be discarded. Sometimes it is the best information available.
